h: Yaakov's Sleepless Nights in Lavan's House: Tehillim Repairing Desire, Envy and Honor
Yaakov's Sleepless Years in Lavan's House

p: — on the verse "and he lay down in that place" (Bereishis 28:11):
— that he was hidden away in the house of Ever
— that he stayed in Lavan's house
— the fifteen Songs of Ascents, etc.
— "Were it not for Hashem who was with us,
כָּל סֵפֶר תְּהִלִּים הָיָה אוֹמֵר כּוּלֵּי
— he would say the entire Book of Tehillim, etc.
— Now, regarding the house of Ever
— If so, why is the question
— asked about Lavan's house more than about Ever's?
— One must also understand the proof
— for the fifteen Songs of Ascents
— "Were it not for Hashem who was with us," etc.
— However, it is because Yaakov's stay in Lavan's house
— and to the darkness of the generations;
— and certainly then, even at night,
— his heart did not lie down,

paragraphs.text: Bereshit Rabbah 68:11: “‘And he lay down in that place’ — Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Nechemyah. Rabbi Yehudah said: Here he lay down, but during all fourteen years that he was hidden away in the house of Ever he did not lie down. Rabbi Nechemyah said: Here he lay down, but during all twenty years that he stayed in Lavan's house he did not lie down. And what would he say? … Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman said: He would say the entire Book of Tehillim. What is the reason? ‘And You are holy, enthroned upon the praises of Israel’ — Israel the Elder.” Rav Tzadok quotes the Midrash nearly word for word; his closing “etc.” (kulei) stands for Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman's proof-verse, Tehillim 22:4, which also reads “Israel” as Yaakov. The same exchange recurs at the end of the parashah, Bereshit Rabbah 74:11 (on “these twenty years”), and in Midrash Tehillim 124:1.

h: Three Holy Traits and Their Opposites

p: — Now, just as the three traits
— are the root of eternal life,
— so too, one corresponding to the other,
— which "remove a person from the world" (Avot 4:21).
— of love — the Chesed of holiness.
— This is Yishmael, the dross of Avraham,
, — as written in the holy Zohar.
— is the opposite of the Gevurah of holiness,
— and it is the dross of Yitzchak:
— whose bed was complete with no dross.
— Nevertheless, there is a refinement of good
— Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him,
— was lowly in his own eyes,
— "I am too small for all the kindnesses" (Bereishis 32:11);
— and he is the root of the Torah of truth,
— whose words leave a high place
— and go to a low place, like water
— And specifically about them it is said,
— Now Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him,
— when he went into exile to the house of Lavan,
— and the root of the opposing side,
וְעַל זֶה אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי
— About this Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said
— that is, to rectify the flaw of desire.
— As in the matter of what is said
— descending from the Court of Israel
— corresponding to the fifteen Songs of Ascents
— when they conduct themselves in holiness,
— the yud in ish (man) and the heh in ishah (woman)
— of this world and of the World to Come.
— to the completeness of the World to Come,
— and that is in the man,
— which is "a tree of life to those who grasp it" (Mishlei 3:18).
— to the completeness of the life of this world,
— which is not through Torah study itself
— "by bringing their sons to the synagogue to learn," etc.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Peri Tzadik, Kuntres Amalah shel Torah 5 (Rav Tzadok): the same identification of Yishmael: “like Yishmael, who is the dross that issued from the trait of Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him, who is full of adultery, evil desires and evil ‘kindnesses,’ and therefore he is called ‘the arrogant waters.’” It joins the two halves of this os in one sentence (Yishmael's desire = the “arrogant waters” of Tehillim 124:5) and adds that the generation of the Flood and Egypt at the Sea drowned in water, the measure of an excess of chesed they could not receive.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 192b (Balak): Rav Tzadok gives no exact location. A close parallel appears in the following Zohar passage: when the Torah is offered to the angel of the right-hand “arm” (Yishmael's line) and he hears “You shall not commit adultery,” he cries: “Woe! Would the Holy One, blessed be He, take this inheritance from me? … For I have received the blessing of water, the blessing of the fish of the sea, as it is written, ‘Be fruitful and multiply’ … and it is written, ‘I will make him fruitful and multiply him’ … and it is written, ‘And he shall be a wild man.’” His whole dominion is the “blessing of water,” the fruitfulness promised to Yishmael, which adultery-free Torah would take from him. This fits both Rav Tzadok's claim here and his linking of Yishmael's desire with the “arrogant waters” in the later discussion of David and the deep; but since he does not cite a page, the identification is not certain.

paragraphs.text: Shir HaShirim Rabbah 4:7:1: “‘You are all fair, my beloved’ — this is Yaakov Avinu, whose bed was complete before him, and no dross was found in it”: “his bed was complete, with no dross found in it.” The idea comes from the very Midrash that opens the os, Bereshit Rabbah 68:11: “From Avraham there issued dross, Yishmael and all the sons of Keturah; from Yitzchak there issued Esav and all his chiefs; but I … I know that no dross will issue from me.” Hence Yishmael is “the dross of Avraham” and Esav “the dross of Yitzchak,” while Yaakov's opposite (honor) is not a son but a trait.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Vayishlach 4:1: “The Midrash says: ‘If you ask why He created the evil inclination … you say that it is evil … the Holy One, blessed be He, said: You are the one who makes it evil.’ That is, the evil inclination was created for good, and only man spoils it and makes it evil. For the root of the evil inclination is envy, desire and honor, and all of them are needed in holiness as well. Envy: we find (Bava Basra 21a), ‘The envy of scribes increases wisdom.’ Desire: it is said in Midrash HaNe'elam (Zohar I 138a), ‘Were it not for the evil inclination, there would be no joy in Torah study.’ And honor too exists in holiness, as in the verse, ‘His heart was lofty in the ways of Hashem’ (II Divrei HaYamim 17:6): one needs loftiness of heart, to know that through his deeds he acts upon all the worlds, and thereby he walks in the ways of Hashem. This resembles pride, yet it is in holiness.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Vayishlach 4 states as a general rule what this os says of honor, that each of the three traits that “remove a person from the world” has a holy form. It also names the holy form of honor: knowing that one's deeds act upon the upper worlds. Here Rav Tzadok locates it instead in the honor that comes to the humble.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 2:1: “‘And the arrogant’ corresponds to the kelipah of honor, which is self-elevation and haughtiness, as it says, ‘A proud, haughty man, scoffer is his name’ (Mishlei 21:24). It stands against the holiness of the Torah, which in holiness is called honor, as they said, ‘There is no honor but Torah, as it says, “The wise shall inherit honor.”’ Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, whose image is engraved on the Throne of Glory, merited this, for he was a ‘dweller of tents,’ meaning the tents of Torah, and ‘the voice is the voice of Yaakov’ in Torah; and this is the trait of ‘truth to Yaakov,’ as they said (Berachos 5b), ‘Truth is Torah, as it says, “Buy truth.”’ … Yaakov Avinu merited the Torah through his lowliness in his own eyes, as it says, ‘I am too small for all the kindnesses,’ and it says, ‘Yaakov, for he is small’; for words of Torah leave a high place and go to a low place, and haughtiness is a sign of poverty in Torah (Kiddushin 49b).”

It adds that Torah is itself the “honor” and the “truth” of Yaakov, and sets this against the Greeks' haughtiness, the “arrogant” of Al HaNissim.

h: David, the Deep, and the Fifteen Ascents

— for it will be whitened in the Future to Come;

paragraphs.text: Sukkah 53a: “Thus it was stated: When David dug the foundations of the altar, the deep rose up and sought to flood the world”; continued on Sukkah 53b: “When he saw that it sank too far, he said: The higher it rises, the more the world is moistened. He recited the fifteen Ascents and raised it fifteen thousand cubits, and set it at a thousand cubits.” The passage opens on 53a with Rav Chisda's question “these fifteen Songs of Ascents — on what occasion did David say them?”; the words Rav Tzadok quotes from “the higher it rises” onward are on 53b.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Sod Yesharim, Sukkot 74 (Ishbitz–Radzin): R. Gershon Chanoch of Radzin explains the same Gemara (Sukkah 53a): “In the deep Hashem, blessed be He, placed the greatest preciousness,” and every good influence in this world comes from raising the deep; David's digging was the wish to reveal that buried treasure. It shares the reading of the deep as hidden good, without Rav Tzadok's link to desire.

h: Three Camps, Three Impurities, Three Flaws

p: — about sending out from three camps,
— the zav, the metzora, and one impure through a corpse —
— comes for the flaw of evil speech,
— which stems from envy and anger;
— and that is the trait of Esav,
— which has no rectification at all,
— even in the Future to Come,
— "And there shall be no survivor," etc. (Ovadyah 1:18).
— "the anger of the Sages, which is good," etc.,
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב, קפב עַמּוּד ב)
— that is only in this world,
כָּל זְמַן שֶׁזַּרְעוֹ שֶׁל עֲמָלֵק קַיָּם
— as long as the seed of Amalek exists;
— But in the Future to Come,
— when the seed of Amalek will perish,
— nothing of this will remain at all,
— and it will have no rectification whatsoever.
— Therefore the metzora is sent out
— even from the camp of Israel,
— no elevation in holiness at all.
— This is not so of the zav,
— who corresponds to the flaw of desire:
— he is not sent out of the camp of Israel,
— because desire has an elevation in holiness,
— he is sent out only from the Levite camp,
— for he has no cleaving to holiness;
— from what is said, "and they shall join you" (Bamidbar 18:2).
— And one impure through the dead is alluded to
— as corresponding to the flaw of honor and self-elevation.
— the essence of the breaking and the death
— as it says, "Hashem reigns; He is clothed in majesty" (Tehillim 93:1).
— For He needed, as it were,
— for the sake of the Kingdom of Heaven;
— the aspect of "the primordial kings who died,"
שֶׁכָּל אָדָם שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ גַּסּוּת הָרוּחַ
— that any person who has arrogance
— is as though he worships idols.
— of ruling over the whole world,
— he said, "I will ascend above the heights of the clouds;
— I will be like the Most High" (Yeshayahu 14:14).

— which are the flaws of anger and self-elevation,

— the revelation of His Kingship, may He be blessed,

— and he had a great comprehension,

paragraphs.text: Bamidbar Rabbah 19:6 and Midrash Tanchuma, Chukat 8: “Things not revealed to Moshe were revealed to Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues; ‘and every precious thing his eye has seen’ (Iyov 28:10) — this is Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues.” The same passage opens with “There shall be no light, yekarot and kippa'on”: “Things that are concealed from you in this world are destined to be visible to you in the World to Come” — the verse of Pesachim 50a, which is why Rabbi Akiva, who saw now what others will see only then, could deal with what is “weighty in this world.”

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 101b: “Achitofel saw tzara'at appearing on his member; he thought that he himself would reign, but it was not so: it was Bat Sheva his daughter, from whom Shlomo would issue”: the Gemara too says “his daughter,” though Bat Sheva was the daughter of Eliam son of Achitofel — the English therefore clarifies the relationship as “granddaughter.”

p: — And this too was the intent
— of King David, peace be upon him,
— in asking that it be considered —
— like engaging in Nega'im and Ohalot:
— that is, that it be possible
— which are severe and weighty in this world.
— the statement of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman
— that the entire Book of Tehillim
— Yaakov would say in Lavan's house.
— For certainly he labored there to rectify
— those of envy and honor too,
— just like the flaw of desire
— according to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi;
— all three flaws for all generations,
— the root of life in holiness,
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נִשְׁרָשׁ עַל יְדֵי זֶה בָּנוּ
— so that thereby there be rooted in us
— the three traits of the holy Avos.
— For in the meal of the Field of Apples (Chakal Tapuchin),
— the flaw of desire is rectified;
— for "he dwelt in the land of the Negev" (Bereishis 24:62),
— from all the desires of the world.
— And in the meal of Atika Kadisha,
— the flaw of anger and envy is rectified;
— for the trait of Avraham Avinu
— was that he was clean and purified
— of the aspect of Gevurot entirely.
— And in the third meal, that of Ze'ir Anpin,
— the flaw of self-elevation is rectified.
— lowliness in the very essence of his soul,
— as it says, "I am too small," etc.,

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Shem MiShmuel, Vayetzei 2:14 (Chassidus): the Sochatchover reads the same Midrash: the fifteen Songs are the fifteen steps from the Women's Court (receiving) to the Court of Israel (giving), Yaakov's ascent in Lavan's house; and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman's “the whole Tehillim” means his labor there was for all his descendants — as Rav Tzadok says, “for all generations.”

paragraphs.text: “And Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman said he would say the entire Book of Tehillim: that his labor and his ascents were not for himself alone, but to open a gateway for all his descendants after him, and the rectification of all events.”

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 88a–b (Yitro): “When Rabbi Abba sat at the Shabbat meal … he would say: This is the holy meal of Atika Kadisha, the most hidden of all”: the Zohar names the three Shabbat meals after the Field of Holy Apples, Atika Kadisha and Ze'ir Anpin. The pairing of each meal with one of the Avos, and of each with one of the three flaws, is Rav Tzadok's own (see the parallels below).

paragraphs.text: Genesis 24:62: “And Yitzchak came from the way of Be'er Lachai Ro'i, and he dwelt in the land of the Negev.” Rav Tzadok reads Negev as “dried out”; in Peri Tzadik, Pekudei 6 he gives the source, Temurah 16a: “‘For you have given me the land of the Negev’ (Yehoshua 15:19) — a house dried out of all good.”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Peri Tzadik, Shmini 9 (Rav Tzadok): the three Shabbat meals as the repair of envy, desire and honor, and Yaakov's meal against pride because he said “I am too small”; it also cites the Zohar (Midrash HaNe'elam, Zohar I 137a) that desire will be called Lavan in the future and the joy of Torah (138a). But there the night meal (Yitzchak) repairs envy and the morning meal (Avraham) desire — the reverse of this os.

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Pekudei 6 (Rav Tzadok): agrees with this os: Yitzchak, “dried out” in the land of the Negev, stands against the kelipah of Yishmael (desire), Avraham, who loved people, against Esav (envy), and Yaakov's “I am too small” against pride.
